blurb: The culinary burnet: a low, ferny rosette of toothed pinnate leaflets whose young leaves taste unmistakably of cucumber, over wiry stems carrying small round green heads tufted with crimson styles. Alone among the burnets it genuinely thrives here — xeric, lime-loving and tough enough that the Intermountain West seeds it by the pound for rangeland forage — and it holds green foliage through most of a Front Range winter.
size: ~9 in–2 ft tall × 1–2 ft wide (6 in on droughty ground, to ~25 in where irrigated)
sun: Full sun (6+ hours); tolerates only light shade before it grows lax
water: Low; genuinely xeric once the taproot is down — an occasional deep soak only to keep the leaves tender for the kitchen
spread: Clumping from a woody caudex and deep taproot, sometimes weakly rhizomatous — but it self-sows freely and naturalizes; deadhead before seed set and site it away from wild land
seasons: Ferny blue-green rosettes push very early in spring; wiry stems of round green heads tufted crimson from late spring into summer; the basal foliage stays green and usable well into winter until heavy snow flattens it
wildlife: Wind-pollinated and petal-less, so a minor pollinator plant (bees do work it for pollen); its real value is wildlife food — high-protein browse for deer, elk and antelope and seed for birds through fall and winter
deer: NOT deer-resistant — rated very desirable browse for deer, elk and antelope, though it regrows readily from the caudex
toxic: No toxicity reported; listed non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses
origin: Europe, western Asia, Siberia & northern Africa (incl. the Canary Islands)
habitat: Lean chalk and limestone grassland, dry meadows and well-drained disturbed ground

care.hardiness: Rated roughly USDA 4a–8b, so it is comfortably hardy through Boulder's zone 5b–6a, and it has excellent cold-winter tolerance on top of that.[4][1] It is well adapted from about 1,000 to 6,000 ft — in Utah it is found at 5,000–7,000 ft, right around Front Range elevations — and it is genuinely long-lived, with plants known to persist more than 20 years on western rangelands.[1][2]
care.planting: Set nursery plants out in spring once the soil is workable, or right after the mid-May last frost; direct seeding is best done late fall through very early spring so winter moisture carries germination.[1] Give it a sunny, sharply drained spot — it does not tolerate poor drainage, flooding or a high water table, so avoid low clay pockets and irrigated turf edges.[1] In a container use a free-draining mix with some grit, water at the base rather than overhead, and expect to water far more often than in the ground; a pot also sidesteps our high-pH, low-organic-matter soils if you would rather not amend a bed.[5]
care.sun: Full sun — six or more hours of direct light, and on the Front Range a west or south exposure is ideal.[4][5] It will tolerate minor semi-shade, but the selected forage strains are explicitly not shade-tolerant, and in shade the rosette opens up, flops and yields fewer of the tender leaves you actually want.[1]
care.soil: It does best on well-drained, frankly infertile or disturbed soil — the opposite of a pampered herb bed.[1] It is most productive on slightly acidic to mildly alkaline ground and tolerates pH up to about 8.0 plus mildly saline conditions, which is exactly why it shrugs off Boulder's alkaline clay where most Sanguisorba sulk.[3] Clay, sand and high-organic-matter soils all work provided drainage is good.[4] Colorado soils run low in organic matter, so a modest compost amendment worked in before planting helps the seedbed without pushing the soft, floppy growth that richness causes.[5]
care.water: Genuinely drought tolerant: a long, stout taproot stores water and the plant adjusts its water-use efficiency as conditions change, so an established clump needs essentially no supplemental irrigation in an average Boulder year.[3] It establishes in areas receiving as little as 12 in of annual precipitation, though it generally does not persist below 14 in — Boulder's ~20 in is comfortably above that.[1] For kitchen use, though, an occasional deep soak in the hottest weeks keeps the leaves tender rather than tough. Water at the base with drip rather than overhead, which spreads foliar disease on herbs.[5]
care.spacing: Space plants about 12–18 in apart (allow 12 in to 3 ft of room per plant) so the mounds knit into a low edging without shading each other.[4] If you are growing it for seed rather than salad, the row spacing used in production fields is 30–42 in to allow cultivation between rows.[1]
care.propagation: Easiest from seed, which germinates readily — commercial lots run 90–95% germination — but established clumps can also be divided in spring.[3][4] Seedlings have excellent vigor yet the plant establishes slowly: expect leaves the first season and no real flowering until at least the second growing season, which is also when it first sets seed.[1][3] Because it self-sows so freely, volunteer seedlings around a parent plant are the simplest source of replacements.
care.sow: Sow late fall to very early spring into a firm, weed-free seedbed so the seed gets natural winter moisture; late-summer sowing is not recommended unless the site is irrigated.[1] Germination normally happens in the first growing season if moisture is adequate, but stands establish slowly and benefit from weed control, mulching and a little irrigation while they fill in.[1] Because burnet is a broadleaf, do not reach for 2,4-D to clean up weeds in a new stand — mow weeds at or before bloom instead.[1]
care.depth: Sow ¼–¾ in deep into a firm seedbed (drilled, or broadcast and lightly covered); it is not a surface-sown seed.[1]
care.bloom: Growth starts very early in spring and the flower stalks follow from late May through June, extending into July in cooler seasons and higher country.[1][2] The 'flowers' are petal-less green heads with a purple-crimson tinge on upright stalks to about 2 ft: the lower flowers in each head are staminate with about a dozen long, dangling filiform stamens, the upper ones pistillate with feathery crimson styles.[1][4] Despite the odd insect visitor, the species is exclusively wind-pollinated and highly self-compatible — it will even set seed by selfing — so treat the bloom as ornamental and structural, not as a bee buffet.[7]
care.feeding: Essentially none needed — it is adapted to infertile ground and rich feeding just makes soft, floppy, weaker-flavoured growth.[1] A compost amendment at planting is enough in our low-organic-matter soils.[5] Split nitrogen applications in spring and fall plus fall phosphorus are used only to push seed yield in commercial production fields, not in a garden.[1]
care.maintenance: About as low-maintenance as an herb gets.[4] Shear the flower stalks off at the base as they go over — it keeps the plant tidy, pushes fresh leaves and stops the seeding.[4] Harvest or shear no more than a third of the plant at a time.[5] The foliage stays green and edible through most of the winter until heavy snow cover, so leave it standing rather than cutting it down in fall; comb out the tattered old leaves in early spring instead.[1] A straw mulch before the first hard frost and occasional winter watering during our dry spells are standard Front Range insurance for perennial herbs.[5]
care.selfsow: This is the honest caveat: burnet establishes and spreads relatively quickly by seed, and while it is generally not classed as weedy it can move into adjoining plant communities under favourable conditions, with reports of invasive weedy behaviour in Wyoming.[1] It builds a persistent soil seed bank whose seed stays viable at least 30 years, so a few seasons of letting it go are not easily undone.[3] Prairie and oak-habitat land managers in the Pacific Northwest have flagged salad burnet as an emerging invasive threat in their ecoregion, where nearly all North American plants are subsp. muricata.[6][3] It is not on any Colorado noxious weed list (verified against CDA Lists A/B/C, the Watch List and the state Noxious Weed Seed List, 2026-07-28), but the sensible practice is unchanged: cut the flower stalks before seed sets, pull volunteers you did not want, and do not plant it against open space or wild grassland.
care.troubles: No serious pests or diseases, and disease problems are described as minimal.[4][1] Grasshoppers and other insects can chew new stands, and rodents and wildlife will graze young plants before they are established.[1] The real killers are cultural: poor drainage, flooding or a high water table rot the crown and taproot.[1] Keep water off the foliage — splashing irrigation is how foliar disease moves through an herb bed — and use drip at the base.[5] In shade or rich soil expect a floppy, sparse plant with coarser-tasting leaves.[1]
care.harvest: Pick the young, tender leaflets from the outside of the rosette, ideally before the flower stalks rise — older leaves turn tough and bitter, and young foliage has by far the better flavour.[4] Harvest in the morning after the dew has dried, and never take more than a third of a perennial at once.[5] Cutting the flower stalks back triggers a fresh flush of mild leaves, and because the rosette stays green well into winter you can pick from it long after the rest of the herb bed is done.[4][1] Use it fresh — the cucumber flavour is delicate and does not survive drying — in salads, vinegars, butters and soft cheeses.[1][4]

edible.card: Young leaves, fresh — cool cucumber flavour
edible.summary: A genuine culinary herb: the young leaves taste distinctly of cucumber and are used fresh in salads, vinegars, butters and soft cheeses.[1][4]
edible.parts: The young, tender leaflets are the edible part — nothing else on the plant is used as food. Older leaves and the flowering stems turn tough and bitter, so the useful window is the fresh growth in the rosette, which on the Front Range means most of spring and fall plus much of a mild winter.[4][1]
edible.preparation: Use it raw and fresh; the cucumber note is delicate and largely cooks or dries away. Strip the leaflets from the wiry midrib and toss them whole or roughly chopped into green salads, or steep them in vinegar, butter, cottage or cream cheese, iced drinks and cold soups — the classic uses recorded for the herb.[1][4][8]
edible.caution: Salad burnet is not reported to be toxic and NC State lists it as non-toxic to dogs, cats and horses, but a few rules matter.[4] Eat the young leaves only: the foliage is high in tannins (measured at roughly 59–130 mg catechin-equivalents per gram of extract) and mature leaves get markedly astringent, tough and bitter, so 'more' is not better — it is a seasoning green, not a bulk salad base.[8][4] The same tannins underlie its traditional use as an astringent and styptic remedy; that is a medicinal history, not a licence to consume concentrated extracts or large quantities.[8] Do not forage naturalized stands on rangeland, pasture or roadsides: this species is deliberately seeded for forage and is also actively controlled with broadleaf herbicides such as 2,4-D, dicamba, metsulfuron, clopyralid and picloram, so wild-looking colonies may have been sprayed — harvest only from plants you grew.[1] Finally, identify what you are picking: several other burnets exist (including native Sanguisorba species), and only this one is the established cucumber-flavoured salad herb.[1]
